title: The Character I Almost Overlooked: Abner
paragraphs: The Character I Almost Overlooked: Abner
Most people read past Abner.

He is rarely the sermon title. Rarely the poster. Rarely the man anyone stops for.
Not David. Not Saul. Not Samuel. Not even Joab.
Abner feels like background.

But here’s what most people don’t realize: some of the most dangerous people in Scripture are not always the loudest rebels. Sometimes they are the powerful men standing close to the truth… while never fully surrendering to it.
And that is why Abner matters.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior, this is one of those overlooked biblical portraits that exposes the heart with uncomfortable precision.
Abner was strong. Influential. Respected. Political. Necessary.

He was “the commander of Saul’s army” (1 Samuel 14:50), a man of rank, proximity, and military weight. He stood near the throne. He knew the movements of kings. He understood power. He could shape outcomes.
But being near the kingdom is not the same as belonging to the King.
Read that again.

Abner spent much of his life defending a house God had already rejected. Scripture says, “Now the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul” (1 Samuel 16:14). That should stop you. Because Abner kept lending his strength to a collapsing kingdom, fighting to preserve what God had already judged.
How many people are doing that right now?

Still defending what God has left.
Still protecting what God has exposed.
Still building on pride, reputation, control, lust, ego, and self-rule—while calling it wisdom.

The tragedy of Abner is not that he lacked intelligence.
The tragedy is that he used his gifts to uphold the wrong throne.
Second Samuel says, “There was a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David. And David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul became weaker and weaker” (2 Samuel 3:1).
That verse is bigger than politics. It is spiritual.

Anything built against God’s chosen King will weaken, no matter how impressive it looks at first. That includes human pride. That includes religious performance. That includes the version of you that wants blessings without surrender.
And this is where the story gets even heavier.

Abner knew David was rising. He was not blind. In fact, later he confessed what had long been obvious: “The Lord has promised David, saying, ‘By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel’” (2 Samuel 3:18).
He knew.

He knew what God had said.
He knew who God had chosen.
He knew where history was going.
But knowledge alone does not save anyone.

You can know truth and still resist it.
You can quote Scripture and still protect self.
You can recognize God’s hand and still delay obedience.
That delay is deadly.

Because Abner did not move toward David out of pure worship or broken repentance at first. He moved after offense, conflict, and wounded pride. When Ish-bosheth challenged him, Abner’s anger flared, and then he decided to transfer his loyalty (2 Samuel 3:6–10). That is sobering. He changed direction, yes—but not from a clean heart.

A lot of people turn only when ego gets bruised.
Not because sin is hated.
Not because God is holy.
Not because Christ is beautiful.
But because their idol stopped paying them back.
And still—this is where the Bible becomes terrifyingly honest and breathtakingly merciful—God’s purposes keep moving.

Even through damaged motives.
Even through compromised men.
Even through the ruins of ambition.
But do not miss the warning: influence without surrender is not faithfulness.

Abner had access. He had strength. He had strategic value. He could negotiate kingdoms. Yet for all his importance, he remains a picture of a man who stood close to God’s unfolding plan without being remembered as a model of wholehearted devotion.
That should shake every churchgoer who confuses involvement with obedience.

You can serve around holy things and still have an unsurrendered heart.
You can stand near David and miss the deeper need for redemption.
You can talk kingdom language while still being ruled by self.
And self-rule is the ancient poison.

Scripture does not flatter us. “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). Not some. All. The polished and the broken. The public sinner and the hidden manipulator. The rebel in the street and the respectable man in the war room.
Sin is not merely failure. It is rebellion against God. It is the enthronement of self.
That is why Abner’s story is not just about Abner.

It is about you.
It is about me.
It is about every heart that knows enough to be accountable but resists full surrender.
But here is where the story must turn—because the Bible never leaves the broken soul with diagnosis alone.
David, for all his significance, was never the final answer. He points forward. Beyond the battlefield. Beyond the throne of Israel. Beyond the political tension of 2 Samuel.
He points to Jesus Christ, the true and better King.

The Son of David.
The rejected King who is still God’s chosen King.
The One many overlook until it is too late.

John writes, “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11). Like David in his rise, Jesus was resisted by those clinging to threatened kingdoms. Yet unlike every earthly king, Jesus came not merely to claim a throne but to save sinners.
And this is the heart of the Gospel.

We have all sided with the wrong kingdom.
We have all loved self more than God.
We have all sinned.
We deserve judgment.
“The wages of sin is death,” Romans 6:23 says, “but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
Read that again.

Death is earned.
Grace is given.
And eternal life is not found in your effort, morality, family background, church activity, or biblical literacy. It is found in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Jesus lived the righteous life we failed to live. He died the death our sins deserved. “But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Then He rose again in victory, proving sin, death, and hell do not get the final word.

So the call is not, “Try harder.”
The call is not, “Become more impressive.”
The call is not, “Use your influence better so God will accept you.”
The call is: repent and believe the Gospel.
Scripture says, “Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 3:19). And again: “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved” (Acts 16:31).
That is the line Abner’s story presses on your soul.

Will you keep strengthening the house God has rejected—your pride, your secret sin, your image, your self-made identity?
Or will you bow before the true King?
If this found you, it’s not by accident.

Maybe you have been near truth for years.
Maybe you know the verses.
Maybe you can identify the kingdom language.
Maybe, like Abner, you recognized God’s direction long ago but have not fully yielded.

Do not mistake delayed movement for obedience.
Do not confuse awareness with repentance.
Do not stand near the kingdom while resisting the King.
Jesus Christ is the only answer.
And here is the mercy that still stands open tonight:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

Not partially.
Not reluctantly.
Not after you fix yourself.
By grace. Through faith. In Jesus Christ alone.

So do not just admire the lesson in Abner.
Let it confront you.
Let it expose you.
Let it drive you to the cross.
Because the overlooked character is revealing the overlooked danger: a heart close to the story of God, but not yet surrendered to the Son of God.
And that can change right now.
